stations.title: Object Detective
steps: Hold things from the box up to the camera. Which ones does the AI recognise, which ones not?
Push the “How sure does the AI have to be?” slider all the way to the left. What nonsense suddenly pops up?
Push it all the way to the right. What does the AI miss now?
stations.rally: Find an object the AI recognises with over 80% — and one it ignores completely.
stations.think: The AI knows exactly 80 things. Who decided that — and what does it mean for everything it doesn’t know?

stations.title: Train the AI
steps: Pick two objects. Give them real names on the screen (tap the name).
Capture 8–10 examples of each — from different angles and distances!
Test it: does the AI recognise both reliably?
stations.rally: The bias experiment: train it badly on purpose — capture one thing only from the front, the other only from the back. Then turn both around. What happens, and what is this problem called in real AIs?
stations.think: Here you can delete all the data at the push of a button. Where on the internet would you like that too?

stations.title: Privacy Shield
steps: Look into the camera — your face is made unrecognisable straight away.
Try all three shield styles. Switch the shield off for a moment: how does the difference feel?
Test the limits: turn your head, hand over half your face, sunglasses…
stations.rally: Find two ways the shield fails. Write it down: why is that a problem for a “protection promise”?
stations.think: Detection (“there is a face”) is not recognition (“that is Ali from class 8B”). Why does this difference matter so much?

stations.title: The Data Trail
steps: Open the station and look at the heat map. This data was collected on the side while you were playing!
Walk a particular route as a group — can you see your trail appear?
Press “Erase the data trail”. Who should have that button in real life?
stations.rally: Name three things you could read off a map like this about a room and its people — with no faces at all.
stations.think: “I’ve got nothing to hide” — does that hold for your walking routes, your habits, your favourite corner too?

stations.title: Fool the AI
steps: The four challenges are on the screen: Invisible 🥷 · Mix-up 🎩 · Bullseye 💯 · Ghosts 👻
stations.rally: Crack at least two challenges and note down how — your trick is the insight!
stations.think: You outsmarted an AI in a few minutes. What does that mean for places where AIs decide on their own — border control, job applications, self-driving cars?

stations.title: Skeleton Mirror
steps: Stand in front of the camera — you turn into a stick figure with 17 points.
Play the pose course: who can do all four poses fastest?
Switch on Ghost mode: no more video, just skeletons. Can you still tell who is who?
stations.rally: In ghost mode, find three things you can work out about a person even though you never see their face.
stations.think: Games consoles, fall sensors in care homes, pool cameras that spot someone drowning — all skeleton tracking. When is it care, when is it surveillance? And who decides that?

discussion.title: The smart doorbell
discussion.scenario: The Yilmaz family has a camera doorbell. It automatically films the pavement too — so all the neighbours, the postal worker, kids playing. The recordings end up on the manufacturer’s servers in the USA.
discussion.ask: Whose privacy counts here? What would you change if you got to build the doorbell? (Tip: today you saw a camera that makes faces unrecognisable before anything is stored…)

discussion.title: The stadium
discussion.scenario: A football stadium wants face recognition at the entrance: known violent offenders are to be spotted automatically. To do that, every face of all 50,000 visitors is scanned and compared against a database.
discussion.ask: 49,990 uninvolved people get scanned to find 10 — fair or not? And what if the AI gets it wrong (you know by now that it does)?

discussion.title: The school camera
discussion.scenario: Your school is thinking about putting up AI cameras that are supposed to report “suspicious behaviour” — scuffles, vandalism. Supposedly nothing is stored, only an alarm is sent.
discussion.ask: Would you feel safer — or watched? Does a camera change how you behave, even if it “stores nothing”? (Think back to The Data Trail station!)

discussion.title: The free filter
discussion.scenario: A photo app makes funny AI filters — for free. In the small print: all uploaded faces may be used to train new AI models.
discussion.ask: Today you trained an AI yourself — with data you could delete afterwards. Why don’t most apps offer that? What would be a fair trade for a free filter?

discussion.title: The supermarket
discussion.scenario: A supermarket uses cameras to count anonymously where customers walk and where they stop — like our heat map, no faces. Shelves get rearranged and prices placed to match.
discussion.ask: Is that okay because nobody is identifiable? Where does the line run for you between “anonymous statistics” and “manipulation”?

discussion.title: You’re in charge
discussion.scenario: Imagine: you get to write the rules for all AI cameras in your city. Today you saw what is possible — detecting, tracking, but also protecting and deleting.
discussion.ask: Write down three rules together that every AI camera would have to follow. Compare with the other groups: which rule comes up everywhere?
